episode_title: #126 Stop Building Agents, Design Workflows Instead – with Ravi Parimi, GTM & RevOps Leader

real_qa.q: Why is agent-first mindset wrong for deploying AI in production sales workflows?
real_qa.r: Agent-first mindset works for experimentation to test capabilities and limits, but when deploying into production, it fails because production is fundamentally about workflows—sequences of processes with inputs, outputs, people, and systems. Putting an agent on top of an existing inefficient human-only process without redesigning the workflow itself is wrong. Instead, companies must think workflow-first: map out end-to-end processes, define input-output contracts, identify where humans should be involved for exceptions and judgment, and deterministically specify rules for agents to execute without hallucination.

real_qa.q: What is the difference between using agents for task automation versus designing workflows with agents?
real_qa.r: Task-based agent development is first-generation thinking—agents write emails, summarize drafts, generate documents. But when thinking from outcomes and jobs to be done, you need a series of sequential steps. Lead routing exemplifies this: you must consider disputes on account ownership, strategic account handling, non-standard terms, and edge cases where humans apply judgment. Agents must be treated as digital workers in a talent mix, not standalone tools, with clear understanding of agent capabilities versus human capabilities within each workflow step.
real_qa.requete: agent task automation vs workflow design RevOps

real_qa.q: How should companies manage agent autonomy and permissions in production workflows?
real_qa.r: Autonomy should have a renewable license with clearly defined scope and permissions. Agents must have conditions specifying when they are allowed to decide and when they are allowed to execute steps. The analogy is a driver's license: you are not allowed to drive every vehicle under every condition—permissions vary by vehicle type and context. Similarly, agents need clearly defined permissions under which they can execute and perform, with human oversight built into the workflow design.

real_qa.q: What happens to RevOps workflows after an agent is deployed to production?
real_qa.r: Work does not stop at agent launch. Deploying something to production does not mean work is done. Someone must own agent operations post-launch, taking responsibility for speed, quality, cost, latency, and ongoing improvement. This requires a product-centric mindset: thinking about releases, roadmaps, agile workflows, sprint-based deployment processes, and performance metrics. Companies must iterate from workflow V1 to V2 to V3 with ownership of benchmarks and KPIs, similar to how DevOps transformed engineering operations.

real_qa.q: Why do RevOps teams need sandbox testing environments and feedback loops for agent workflows?
real_qa.r: Without testing environments and feedback loops, agents can do unintended things without being caught—there are already stories of agents breaking systems. A proper system includes a secure sandbox environment where you can test before production, layered security to prevent unwanted behavior, and feedback mechanisms to train agents further. This mirrors software development practices where you test before release, and should apply equally to AI agents to avoid critical failures like accidental CRM data deletion.
real_qa.requete: agent testing sandbox environment security RevOps

He worked at highly scaled companies including AWS, VMware, and Cisco, as well as SaaS companies like Zendesk and Service Titan. He served as an Executive in Residence at Andreessen Horowitz, advising portfolio companies on scaling operations and go-to-market strategy, and transitioned to GTM operations around 2012-2014 after working in strategy, operations, and engineering operations roles at Deloitte, PwC, and Cisco.
